title: Professional Portfolio
text:
This portfolio collects a series of real projects I have developed at work, with a focus on financial data, treasury workflows, and analytics. The projects are designed to be reproducible and demonstrate my skills in data engineering, analysis, and visualization.
This portfolio is a work in progress, and I will continue to add new projects as they are completed.

title: Professional Portfolio
text:
Projects


Kyriba TMS Transformation
My end-to-end Kyriba Treasury Management System work, covering functional design, core data and access setup, banking and trade integrations, ERP and Data Platform connectivity, and post-go-live optimisation.

title: Daily FX Rates — Project Report
text:
Overview
This report documents the maintained FX rates loader in src/daily_fx_rates.py, which fetches daily FX rates from the Frankfurter API and stores them in a CSV file and Neon PostgreSQL table.
The loader normalizes keys before deduplication, backfills missing business-day rows, and tracks provisional rows with fx_quality_flag so they can be revalidated on later runs.


Setup
pip install -r daily-fx-rates/requirements.txt


Run
Run the maintained loader from the repository root:
python src/daily_fx_rates.py
If you want to render the report itself with Quarto:
quarto render daily-fx-rates/report.qmd


Outputs

daily-fx-rates/data/fx_rates.csv
Neon PostgreSQL (table: fx_rates)



Example

import pandas as pd
from pathlib import Path
from IPython.display import display

p = Path('daily-fx-rates/data/fx_rates.csv')
if p.exists():
    display(pd.read_csv(p).tail())
else:
    print('No fx_rates.csv present; creating a small sample for demonstration:')
    sample = pd.DataFrame({
        'date':['2026-08-06','2026-08-07','2026-08-08'],
        'currency':['USD','EUR','GBP'],
        'fx_to_usd':[1.0,0.91,0.78]
    })
    display(sample)

title: Create Date Table — Project Report
text:
Overview
This mini-project creates and maintains a date_table in PostgreSQL, providing a canonical calendar dimension for reporting.


Setup
Ensure DATABASE_URL is available in the repository .env file.
pip install -r create-date-table/requirements.txt


Run
From the repository root:
python create-date-table/create_date_table.py


Table schema
The script generates a table with calendar_date, year, month, quarter, weekday, is_weekend, is_month_start, is_month_end, and ISO week/year.


Notes
The script is idempotent and inserts only missing dates, making it safe for scheduled incremental runs in CI.


Example: preview calendar rows (safe local sample if DB not available)

title: FX Prime Brokerage Collateral
text:
This report documents the FX Prime Brokerage Collateral project as a reproducible analysis. It walks through the Python pipeline, renders outputs from the generated CSV files, and connects those calculations to the Power BI semantic model and dashboard.
The project is synthetic and intended for portfolio demonstration and training. It is not a production margin or collateral engine.


Start by importing the required modules and loading the generated CSV files. The find_project_root() function locates the project folder based on the presence of data/ and src/ subfolders. The four datasets are read into a dictionary of DataFrames for later use.
The pipeline produces four core datasets: the FX portfolio, counterparty limits, mark-to-market data, and the final MTM collateral report.

from pathlib import Path

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import pandas as pd
from IPython.display import display


def find_project_root():
    candidates = [Path.cwd(), Path.cwd() / "fx-prime-brokerage-collateral"]
    for candidate in candidates:
        if (candidate / "data").is_dir() and (candidate / "src").is_dir():
            return candidate
    raise FileNotFoundError("Could not locate the FX collateral project folder")


PROJECT_ROOT = find_project_root()
DATA_ROOT = PROJECT_ROOT / "data"

paths = {
    "portfolio": DATA_ROOT / "FX-portfolio" / "portfolio.csv",
    "limits": DATA_ROOT / "Limits" / "limits.csv",
    "mark_to_market": DATA_ROOT / "Mark-to-market" / "mark_to_market_portfolio.csv",
    "mtm_report": DATA_ROOT / "Mark-to-market" / "mtm_report.csv",
}

data = {name: pd.read_csv(path) for name, path in paths.items()}
data["mtm_report"]["report_date"] = pd.to_datetime(data["mtm_report"]["report_date"])
data["portfolio"]["report_date"] = pd.to_datetime(data["portfolio"]["report_date"])

title: FX Prime Brokerage Collateral
text:
Stage 2: derive limits
generate_limits.py creates a limit schedule for each bank and subtracts the portfolio exposure from the limit:
limit_available_usd = credit_limit_usd - counterparty_exposure_usd
This is a control dataset, not a market valuation. It answers: how much unused counterparty capacity remains? If portfolio exposure exceeds the limit, available capacity becomes negative, indicating that no additional trades should be allocated to that bank until capacity is restored. In practice, a limit breach may restrict the bank’s ability to offer additional transactions until exposure drops back within limits.

title: FX Prime Brokerage Collateral
text:
The calculation






flowchart TD
    A[Active portfolio exposure] --> B[Initial Margin<br/>5% of exposure]
    C[Daily MTM / P&L] --> D[Variation Margin]

    B --> E[Collateral Required]
    D --> E

    E --> F[Compare with<br/>Collateral Posted]

    F --> G{Excess / Deficit}

    G -->|Deficit| H[Schedule next-day posting]
    H --> I[Exposure + buffer]

    G -->|Surplus| J{Above recall buffer?}
    J -->|Yes| K[Potential collateral recall]
    J -->|No| L[No movement]




Figure 3: Collateral Process Flow





The core logic lives in src/generate_mtm_report.py. For each business date:

Initial margin is the minimum amount of cash or collateral deposited with a broker to support a leveraged position. For this synthetic model, initial margin is calculated as 5% of active trade exposure and is stored as a negative amount because it represents an obligation to the broker.
Variation margin is the aggregated mark-to-market P&L. It keeps its market sign: positive means favourable revaluation and negative means adverse revaluation.
Collateral required is the sum of initial margin and variation margin.
Posted collateral is the amount already posted by the client to the broker.
Excess/deficit compares posted collateral with the positive internal obligation. Negative means more collateral is needed; positive means excess collateral is held.
A deficit schedules a next-day posting to reach the exposure plus a buffer (which is normally around $ 500K).
A surplus above the buffer can trigger a collateral recall.

# Simplified calculation from generate_mtm_report.py
im_raw = 0.05 * exposure
vm_raw = daily_pnl
initial_margin = -im_raw
variation_margin = vm_raw
collateral_required = initial_margin + variation_margin
excess_deficit = collateral_required - collateral_posted   
The current constants are INITIAL_COLLATERAL = 1_000_000, BUFFER = 500_000, MOVE_INCREMENT = 10_000, and MIN_MOVE = 50_000.

title: FX Prime Brokerage Collateral
text:
Visualisation: collateral KPI cards
The Power BI dashboard summarises the latest collateral position using KPI cards. The same metrics can be reproduced in Python for validation and comparison. The values retain the data-model sign convention. For example, Initial Margin and Collateral Required remain negative, while the card change shows the ordinary numerical difference from the previous date.

from matplotlib.patches import FancyBboxPatch


def format_amount(value):
    """Format a USD value compactly for a KPI card."""
    absolute_value = abs(value)
    if absolute_value >= 1_000_000:
        return f"{'-' if value < 0 else ''}{absolute_value / 1_000_000:.2f}M"
    if absolute_value >= 1_000:
        return f"{'-' if value < 0 else ''}{absolute_value / 1_000:.0f}K"
    return f"{value:,.0f}"


def format_change(value):
    """Format a numerical daily change with an ASCII direction marker."""
    if value > 0:
        return f"+ {format_amount(value)}"
    if value < 0:
        return f"- {format_amount(abs(value))}"
    return "- 0"


latest_date = mtm_report["report_date"].max()
report_dates = sorted(mtm_report["report_date"].unique())
previous_date = report_dates[-2] if len(report_dates) > 1 else latest_date
latest_report = mtm_report.loc[mtm_report["report_date"] == latest_date].iloc[0]
previous_report = mtm_report.loc[mtm_report["report_date"] == previous_date].iloc[0]

latest_portfolio = portfolio.loc[portfolio["report_date"] == latest_date]
previous_portfolio = portfolio.loc[portfolio["report_date"] == previous_date]

cards = [

text:
Project structure
The checked-in PBIP project is under fx-prime-brokerage-collateral/dashboard/:
dashboard/
├── fx-prime-brokerage-collateral.pbip
├── fx-prime-brokerage-collateral.Report/
│   └── definition/pages/
└── fx-prime-brokerage-collateral.SemanticModel/
    └── definition/
        ├── tables/
        ├── relationships.tmdl
        └── model.tmdl
The model contains three principal facts (fx_portfolio, limits, mtm_report), supporting dimensions (dim_date, dim_banks, dim_currencies), an FX rates table, and Measures_Table for reusable DAX.

title: FX Prime Brokerage Collateral
text:
Relationship and filter design
The date dimension filters mtm_report.report_date, fx_portfolio.report_date, and limits.as_of_date. Bank and currency dimensions provide reusable slicer paths. The collateral page should therefore use dim_date[calendar_date] for time controls rather than placing the fact date directly in every visual.
The primary modelling caveat is grain: mtm_report is daily, while fx_portfolio is trade-leg level. Measures must be used when combining these tables so that a visual does not accidentally sum a daily collateral value once per trade.

title: FX Prime Brokerage Collateral
text:
Core DAX measures
These are the central measures already present in Measures_Table.tmdl:
Initial Margin = SUM(mtm_report[initial_margin])
Variation Margin = SUM(mtm_report[variation_margin])
Collateral Required = SUM(mtm_report[collateral_required])
Collateral Posted = SUM(mtm_report[collateral_posted])
Excess / Deficit = SUM(mtm_report[excess_deficit])
Because initial margin and collateral required are stored as negative amounts owed to the broker, inverse measures can be useful for visuals where positive means amount required.
Initial Margin (Inverse) = -1 * SUM(mtm_report[initial_margin])

Collateral Required (Inverse) = -1 * SUM(mtm_report[collateral_required])

title: FX Prime Brokerage Collateral
text:
Previous-day and moving-average patterns
The previous-day pattern finds the latest fact date before the current date selected in the date dimension, then evaluates the measure at that date:
Collateral Posted (Previous Day) =
VAR CurrentDate = MAX(dim_date[calendar_date])
VAR PreviousDateWithData =
    CALCULATE(
        MAX(mtm_report[report_date]),
        REMOVEFILTERS(dim_date),
        dim_date[calendar_date] < CurrentDate
    )
RETURN
    CALCULATE(
        [Collateral Posted],
        REMOVEFILTERS(dim_date),
        dim_date[calendar_date] = PreviousDateWithData
    )

Collateral Posted (Daily Change) =
    [Collateral Posted] - [Collateral Posted (Previous Day)]
    
For smoothing, the existing model uses a 30-day window:
IM 30 Day Moving Average =
CALCULATE(
    AVERAGEX(
        DATESINPERIOD(
            dim_date[calendar_date],
            MAX(dim_date[calendar_date]),
            -30,
            DAY
        ),
        [Initial Margin (Inverse)]
    )
)

Overview
This Quarto report documents the treasury-cashflow-simulation pipeline: how synthetic daily transactions are generated, internal sweeps applied, CSV outputs produced, and results persisted into PostgreSQL.

pip install -r treasury-cashflow-simulation/requirements.txt


Run

python treasury-cashflow-simulation/run_pipeline.py

title: Kyriba TMS Transformation
section: 1.3 The role: turning treasury intent into system behaviour
text:
1.3 The role: turning treasury intent into system behaviour
My role sat between Treasury operations, Kyriba solution design and hands-on system ownership. I combined functional leadership with technical validation: I translated requirements into specifications, reviewed consultant-designed solutions, tested workflows and mappings, and maintained post-go-live enhancements.


1.3.1 Functional lead
I mapped Treasury requirements to Kyriba capabilities, documented operational needs and challenged existing processes where they created avoidable manual work.


1.3.2 Technical validator
I reviewed workflows, mappings, templates and outputs with implementation teams, banks, custodians, vendors, IT and Finance.


1.3.3 System administrator
I managed enhancements, fixes and optimisation cycles, while escalating technical components that required IT support.

title: Kyriba TMS Transformation
text:
Start with Treasury’s operating reality
Functional design began with Treasury business roles, operational processes and pain points. Stakeholder conversations turned those needs into practical requirements that could be reviewed against Kyriba’s functional capabilities.
The scope included trade processing, banking and payments, FX integration, cash management, accounting, reporting, controls and approvals. The objective was not to treat Kyriba as an isolated application, but to make its behaviour workable for Treasury operations.





flowchart LR

    B --> C[Kyriba functional<br/>specifications]
    C --> D[Functional and<br/>end-to-end testing]


 Requirements-to-solution sequence used for functional design and validation. 





Requirements and alignment
Documented detailed operational requirements, challenged existing processes and identified pain points. Treasury needs were translated into functional specifications.


Workflow and controls
Designed end-to-end Treasury workflows, defined approval and control points, and identified opportunities to simplify manual activity.


Kyriba design and validation
Mapped requirements to Kyriba functionality, reviewed functional behaviour and configuration requirements, and supported functional and end-to-end testing.








TipPart takeaway



Treasury requirements were converted into practical Kyriba solutions while balancing operational needs, controls and system capabilities.

For banking and payments, I supported connectivity setup, statement and payment testing, BTC mapping, reconciliation rules and investigation of breaks in the Bank Connectivity Cockpit. For accounting, I reviewed and improved financial and cash transaction templates with Finance and the Kyriba team. I documented the process from accruals and MTM through GL generation, review and approval. In parallel, I defined Open API requirements with IT and validated outputs through the Data Platform.

Integration work made interfaces observable and testable across Treasury, banks, providers, custodians, Finance, IT and the Data Platform, with exceptions treated as part of the operating process.

    C --> D[Maintain, fix<br/>and optimise]
    D --> A


 Qualitative continuous-improvement loop described by the optimisation work.
